subtopic: Nutrition and mood in general terms
passage:
In Room 214 of the boys' hostel, Sumit's dinner was the same every night: instant noodles at midnight, a packet of chips and a fizzy drink. He skipped the mess because the queue was long, and he usually slept through breakfast. By the end of the month he felt tired all the time, dragged himself to lectures and couldn't be bothered to call home.
One afternoon Nirmala aunty, who ran the mess counter, caught him buying chips. "You look like a wilted spinach leaf," she said. "Come at one tomorrow. I'll keep dal and curd for you."
He went. Then he started taking a banana from the counter on his way out. Some nights it was still noodles, but now he added an egg. After a couple of weeks he noticed he wasn't nodding off in afternoon labs.

qa.q: What did Sumit eat every night at midnight?
qa.a: Instant noodles, with a packet of chips and a fizzy drink.

qa.q: How was Sumit feeling by the end of the month?
qa.a: Sumit felt tired and unmotivated, dragging himself to lectures and not bothering to call home.

qa.q: What small upgrades did Sumit make?
qa.a: Eating dal and curd at the mess, taking a banana on the way out, and adding an egg to the noodles.

qa.q: How might Nirmala aunty see Sumit?
qa.a: Nirmala aunty seems to see a worn-out student who needs looking after, teasing him kindly and keeping food aside.

grounding: A young adult living on late-night instant food feels tired and low, and small upgrades like dal, curd, fruit and eggs help without a perfect diet.

passage:
Hi Ritu Didi,
You asked why I sound so flat on calls. Honestly, I think it's the food. At the PG in Hyderabad, dinner is whatever the delivery app has at 11 pm, usually fried stuff or instant noodles. Lunch is a samosa from the canteen. I've been sleepy in class and grumpy for no reason, and I skipped cricket twice because I just felt heavy.
I remembered what you said about small changes, not a perfect diet. So I've started buying curd and bananas from the shop downstairs, and I asked Mrs Reddy on the ground floor if I could pay for her home-cooked dal-rice three nights a week. She said yes!
It's only been ten days, but I'm less foggy in the mornings. I even went back to cricket.
Love,
Tejas

qa.a: Tejas buys curd and bananas.

qa.a: Ritu Didi would likely feel relieved that Tejas remembered the advice and is feeling less foggy.

subtopic: Nutrition and mood in general terms
passage: Mehak's nursing hostel in Sagar had a canteen, but it closed at eight, and her shifts ended at ten. So dinner was instant noodles in the room, most nights, with crisps from the corner shop. By the second month she was dragging herself through morning lectures, low and heavy, with no energy even to call home. Jomon, who ran the tea stall across the road, noticed her yawning as she bought chai. 'Didi, you look like a ghost. What are you eating?' She laughed. 'Noodles.' 'Every day? Take a banana with your tea. And the dhaba next door keeps dal and roti till eleven.' She tried it: banana in the morning, dal-roti after shift, curd when she could. Not perfect. But after two weeks she noticed she could think in lectures again.

qa.q: What time did the dhaba keep dal and roti till?
qa.a: Till eleven.

qa.q: How was Mehak feeling by the second month?
qa.a: She felt low, heavy and tired, with no energy even to call home.

qa.a: A banana in the morning, dal-roti after her shift and curd when she could.

subtopic: Nutrition and mood in general terms
passage: Clara's first term at university in Leipzig ran on frozen pizza, crisps and coffee. She ate at midnight, skipped lunch and felt too tired to go to the student choir she'd been excited about. Her flatmate Nadia found her asleep at the kitchen table at four in the afternoon. 'You live on beige food,' Nadia said. 'Come on Sunday. I'm making lentil soup, and you can chop.' They cooked a big pot and froze half. Nadia put a bowl of apples on the table and said nothing more. Clara started taking one on her way out, and eating yoghurt instead of crisps at night. It wasn't a transformation. But by December she had the energy to go to choir again, and she sang loudest at the concert.

qa.q: What was Nadia making on Sunday?
qa.a: Lentil soup.

qa.q: How was Clara feeling during her first term?
qa.a: She felt tired and unmotivated, too drained to go to choir.

qa.q: What small changes helped Clara?
qa.a: Cooking lentil soup with Nadia, taking an apple on her way out and eating yoghurt instead of crisps at night.

qa.q: How might Nadia have felt seeing Clara at the concert?
qa.a: Nadia was probably proud and pleased to see her friend energetic again.

grounding: Shows a young adult living on snacks and late food feeling tired and unmotivated, and how small food upgrades lift energy without a perfect diet.

subtopic: Nutrition and mood in general terms
passage: In the engineering hostel mess, the breakfast queue was always short, because most of the boys and girls slept through it. Neelam, twenty-one, was one of them. She lived on late-night instant noodles, chips and a samosa at the college gate. By mid-semester she felt low, sluggish and unable to start assignments. The mess manager, Rehana Ma'am, stopped her one evening. 'You never come for breakfast. There are eggs and bananas every day, and dal at dinner.' Neelam shrugged. 'I'm too tired to get up.' 'Then come just twice a week. Start there.' Neelam tried Tuesdays and Fridays. Eggs, a banana, tea. On those days, she noticed, she could actually focus in the lab. Slowly she added dinner dal. Not every day. But enough to feel less foggy.

qa.q: Which days did Neelam try breakfast at the mess?
qa.a: Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: How was Neelam feeling by mid-semester?
qa.a: She felt low, sluggish and unable to start assignments.

qa.q: Why was Rehana Ma'am's 'twice a week' idea sensible?
qa.a: It was a small, manageable step rather than a demand for a perfect diet, so Neelam could actually start.

qa.q: How might Rehana Ma'am see the students who skip breakfast?
qa.a: She probably sees tired young people missing out on easy food and feels a kind of motherly concern.

grounding: Shows a young adult living on instant snacks and late food feeling tired and low, and how small upgrades like eggs, bananas and dal help without demanding perfection.

Jahnavi
